implementation_notes: The itinerary is a vector of std::function<void(Message&)> carried in the message next to a cursor; type erasure means steps register as plain functions, lambdas or functors without a common base class, and the dispatcher is a three-line loop. This is the C++ default because it needs nothing beyond C++11 and keeps the slip a value that can be copied, moved or built by a planner. A virtual Step base class is still justified when steps need identity, diagnostics or dynamic casting, or when the toolchain cannot use std::function; std::array or a small fixed-capacity vector avoids heap traffic when slip length is bounded.
pitfalls: std::function allocates when a lambda's capture exceeds its small-object buffer, and it owns those captures: a slip stored for later use keeps referenced objects alive (dangling if they were stack temporaries).
Copying the message copies the whole itinerary; hold it as shared_ptr<const std::vector<...>> or move the message.
An exception thrown inside a step unwinds out of the dispatcher with the cursor unadvanced and side effects applied, so steps must be idempotent or the loop has to catch and compensate.

variants.name: C++20 coroutine step chain
variants.idiom_name: task<> advance(Message) with co_await per step
variants.implementation_notes: With C++20 stackless coroutines the callback/loop plumbing disappears: one coroutine owns the message and awaits each step in order (co_await step.run(m)), suspending instead of blocking and resuming when the step completes - including when a step waits on I/O or a remote hop. The roles are unchanged, but the itinerary becomes ordinary control flow, which is why this variant wins in asynchronous services. It requires a coroutine runtime (executor, task type) and C++20 support, and the awaitable step type must own its state across suspension.
pitfalls: State referenced across a suspension point must outlive the coroutine; a slip of awaitables that borrow the message is the coroutine-era dangling-reference bug.
Without an executor owning the coroutine handle, an exception or cancellation leaves the message suspended forever - couple the task type with structured lifetime management.
co_await in a loop hides the progress marker: persist the cursor explicitly if the slip must be resumed after a crash.
